AI agents: perceive, decide and act without constant supervision

They are not digital employees that know everything. They are systems capable of observing information, choosing a next step and using tools to move towards a goal.

By Juliana Gonzalez · September 13, 2026 · 7 min read

Imagine a tool that receives a support request, checks the related information, decides which steps to follow and prepares a response. If it detects that the case requires authorization, it sends it to a person instead of continuing on its own.

This behaviour goes beyond executing a single instruction. The system observes what is happening, evaluates options and takes action to move closer to an objective. That is the essential idea behind an artificial intelligence agent.

An AI agent uses information from its environment to decide what to do and act towards a goal within defined boundaries.

The word autonomous can be misleading. It does not mean the system is independent, has intentions of its own or can act without restrictions. It means it can complete several steps without requesting human instructions for every one.

The fundamental cycle: perceive, decide and act

An agent combines three capabilities that repeat while it performs a task:

1. Perceive

It gathers signals from its environment: text, images, records, search results or data supplied by other tools.

2. Decide

It interprets the available information, compares possibilities and selects the next step that appears most useful.

3. Act

It performs an action, such as querying a system, updating a record, generating content or requesting human intervention.

After acting, the agent can observe the result and begin the cycle again. If a search returns insufficient information, for example, it can reformulate the query. If an action fails, it can try another permitted option or stop.

This cycle does not guarantee that it will always choose correctly. Decision quality depends on the available data, the model being used, the tools it can access and the boundaries that have been established.

A simple example

Consider an agent that helps organize incidents for a web application. Its goal is to prepare each case so the team can handle it more efficiently.

  1. Perceive: it reads the problem description, priority, browser and previous messages.
  2. Decide: it determines whether information is missing and which initial checks would be useful.
  3. Act: it classifies the case, consults documentation or asks the user for a screenshot and reproduction steps.
  4. Evaluate again: it incorporates the new information and decides whether it can suggest a solution or must escalate the case.

A person remains responsible for deciding what information the agent may access, which actions it is allowed to perform and when it must stop.

AI agents and traditional automation are not the same

Traditional automation

It follows a predefined sequence of rules. It works very well when the conditions are known and every situation can be expressed through clear instructions: “if A happens, execute B.”

AI agent

It can interpret less structured information, choose between several steps and adjust its path according to the results it obtains.

This difference does not automatically make an agent the best solution. For a stable, repetitive and verifiable operation, rule-based automation may be faster, less expensive and more predictable.

Not every agent learns permanently over time either. Some adapt their next steps during a task but do not retain that experience afterwards. Continuous learning requires additional memory, evaluation and updating mechanisms.

What they do particularly well

When well designed and working with suitable data, agents can add value by:

  • Processing large volumes of information quickly.
  • Performing routine steps consistently.
  • Monitoring signals and responding without interruption.
  • Coordinating several tools within one workflow.
  • Reducing the manual work required before a human decision.

They could, for example, collect information for a report, check whether a case is missing data or monitor specific events and generate an alert. The benefit is not only doing more; it is freeing time for work that requires judgment, communication and experience.

Their limitations do not disappear because we call them agents

An agent may execute actions, but it still inherits limitations from the models and data it uses:

  • It does not understand social signals, emotions or context in the same way a person does.
  • It does not automatically identify every bias, error or gap in the data.
  • It may misinterpret an ambiguous instruction or pursue a goal in an unexpected way.
  • It can produce a convincing explanation even when its decision is incorrect.
  • It does not automatically know which business, ethical or human consequences are acceptable.

The more power it has to act, the greater the possible impact of an error. Generating a draft is very different from sending an email, changing a database or approving an operation.

Autonomy with human oversight

Designing a responsible agent requires controls before it begins operating. These include minimum necessary permissions, data validation, action logging and clear human approval points.

We should also define when it must stop. An instruction such as “resolve every pending case” is too open-ended. A safer objective specifies which cases it can process, what tools it may use, which changes require confirmation and when it must escalate the work.

Human oversight does not necessarily mean watching every step. It means designing boundaries, reviewing important outcomes and retaining the ability to intervene.

Conclusion

AI agents represent a shift from tools that only generate a response towards systems capable of completing sequences of actions. They perceive information, make decisions and act to reach a goal.

Their value appears in processes that contain variation and require choosing the next step. Their risks also increase when they receive broader permissions or when their decisions affect people and real systems.

The important question is not only “what can this agent do?” but also “what should it be allowed to do, with what information and under which controls?”
